beats.text: There are two ways to get an explanation from a model. You can train a black box and explain it afterwards, which is called post-hoc. Or you can build the model so that its reasoning can be read from the start, which is called ante-hoc, or interpretable by design.
beats.caption: There are two ways to get an explanation from a model. You can train a black box and explain it afterwards, which is called post-hoc. Or you can build the model so that its reasoning can be read from the start, which is called ante-hoc, or interpretable by design.
beats.head: Two routes: explain a model afterwards, or build one you can read

beats.text: Start with post-hoc. The model f is already trained. An explanation method takes the model and one input, and returns some evidence about the prediction.
beats.caption: Start with post-hoc. The model f is already trained. An explanation method takes the model and one input, and returns some evidence about the prediction.
beats.head: Post-hoc: a method explains a {f:trained model} on one {x:input}

beats.text: One family asks which pixels mattered. Start with a tiny example: a three by three image of a vertical bar, and a model that scores three classes: vertical bar, horizontal bar and dot.
beats.caption: One family asks which pixels mattered. Start with a tiny example: a three by three image of a vertical bar, and a model that scores three classes: vertical bar, horizontal bar and dot.
beats.head: Saliency in a tiny example: one {x:image}, three {y:classes}

beats.text: Each class has its own nine weights, and its score is the weighted sum of the pixels. For this image, vertical bar scores 3, dot scores 1.5, and horizontal bar scores 0. So the model says vertical bar.
beats.caption: Each class has its own nine weights, and its score is the weighted sum of the pixels. For this image, vertical bar scores 3, dot scores 1.5, and horizontal bar scores 0. So the model says vertical bar.
beats.head: Each {y:class score} is a weighted sum of the nine {x:pixels}

beats.text: Now brighten the centre pixel by 0.1. The vertical bar and horizontal bar scores each rise by 0.1, and the dot score rises by 0.2. Brighten a corner pixel instead, and the vertical bar score falls by 0.05.
beats.caption: Now brighten the centre pixel by 0.1. The vertical bar and horizontal bar scores each rise by 0.1, and the dot score rises by 0.2. Brighten a corner pixel instead, and the vertical bar score falls by 0.05.
beats.head: Nudge one {x:pixel}, and every {y:class score} moves

beats.text: Divide each change by the size of the nudge. That ratio is the gradient of the class score with respect to the pixel: 1 for vertical bar at the centre, 2 for dot at the centre, and minus 0.5 for vertical bar at a corner. A pixel's saliency is the size of its gradient, ignoring the sign.
beats.caption: Divide each change by the size of the nudge. That ratio is the gradient of the class score with respect to the pixel: 1 for vertical bar at the centre, 2 for dot at the centre, and minus 0.5 for vertical bar at a corner. A pixel's saliency is the size of its gradient, ignoring the sign.
beats.head: Change in score per unit change in pixel: the gradient

beats.text: Do this for all nine pixels and you get a saliency map, and each class has its own. For vertical bar the middle column stands out, for horizontal bar the middle row, and for dot the centre. A saliency map always answers a question about one class.
beats.caption: Do this for all nine pixels and you get a saliency map, and each class has its own. For vertical bar the middle column stands out, for horizontal bar the middle row, and for dot the centre. A saliency map always answers a question about one class.
beats.head: One saliency map for each {y:class}

beats.text: In a deep network the score is no longer a plain weighted sum, so the gradient changes from image to image. Backpropagation computes it for every pixel at once, for one image and one class. Simonyan and colleagues called the result a saliency map.
beats.caption: In a deep network the score is no longer a plain weighted sum, so the gradient changes from image to image. Backpropagation computes it for every pixel at once, for one image and one class. Simonyan and colleagues called the result a saliency map.
beats.head: In a deep network, backpropagation computes the gradient

beats.text: A second family changes the input. Grey out one patch, run the model again, and measure how much the score drops. That is the occlusion map we computed for the gull in Part 1.

beats.text: These methods are useful, and they have limits. The first is a sanity check. If an explanation really describes the model, it should change when the model changes. Adebayo and colleagues tested this by randomising a trained network's weights, layer by layer, until it had learned nothing.
beats.caption: These methods are useful, and they have limits. The first is a sanity check. If an explanation really describes the model, it should change when the model changes. Adebayo and colleagues tested this by randomising a trained network's weights, layer by layer, until it had learned nothing.
beats.head: Limit 1: an explanation should change when the {f:model} changes

beats.text: Some saliency methods, such as guided backpropagation, still produced almost the same maps for the randomised network. Those maps mostly trace the edges in the image, like an edge detector. So a convincing map is not, on its own, evidence about the model. Plain gradients and Grad-CAM did pass this test.
beats.caption: Some saliency methods, such as guided backpropagation, still produced almost the same maps for the randomised network. Those maps mostly trace the edges in the image, like an edge detector. So a convincing map is not, on its own, evidence about the model. Plain gradients and Grad-CAM did pass this test.

beats.text: The second limit is about shortcuts. Zech and colleagues trained a pneumonia detector on chest X-rays from two hospital systems. At one hospital about a third of the patients had pneumonia, and at the other about one in a hundred.
beats.caption: The second limit is about shortcuts. Zech and colleagues trained a pneumonia detector on chest X-rays from two hospital systems. At one hospital about a third of the patients had pneumonia, and at the other about one in a hundred.
beats.head: Limit 2: a model can learn a {k:shortcut}

beats.text: A network could tell which hospital an X-ray came from almost perfectly, from markers and scanner details rather than from the lungs. Since the hospital predicts pneumonia, the detector could use the hospital as a shortcut.
beats.caption: A network could tell which hospital an X-ray came from almost perfectly, from markers and scanner details rather than from the lungs. Since the hospital predicts pneumonia, the detector could use the hospital as a shortcut.

beats.text: A heatmap might light up the hospital marker in the corner, and expose the shortcut. But it cannot remove it. On X-rays from a third hospital, the detector did worse. The only fix was new data and retraining.
beats.caption: A heatmap might light up the hospital marker in the corner, and expose the shortcut. But it cannot remove it. On X-rays from a third hospital, the detector did worse. The only fix was new data and retraining.

beats.text: The third limit is vocabulary. A heatmap says where the score was sensitive. It does not say what the model saw there. On the gull: the yellow bill, the red spot, or the shape of the head?
beats.caption: The third limit is vocabulary. A heatmap says where the score was sensitive. It does not say what the model saw there. On the gull: the yellow bill, the red spot, or the shape of the head?

beats.text: Ante-hoc models take the other route. The prediction is computed from quantities a person can read. A sparse linear model on named features is one example. A short decision tree is another. Prototype networks compare parts of an image with stored example parts.

beats.text: Let us slow down. What exactly is a concept? It is more than a neuron with a name attached: it is a promise that a person can check the claim in the input.
beats.caption: Let us slow down. What exactly is a concept? It is more than a neuron with a name attached: it is a promise that a person can check the claim in the input.
beats.head: A {c:concept} is a claim that a person can check

beats.text: Three things must be in place. The first is meaning: a definition that a domain expert can apply. For example, grey wingtip: the tips of the folded flight feathers are grey, not black.
beats.caption: Three things must be in place. The first is meaning: a definition that a domain expert can apply. For example, grey wingtip: the tips of the folded flight feathers are grey, not black.
beats.head: Meaning: a definition that an expert can apply

beats.text: The second is grounding: where in the input is the evidence? For wingtip colour, it is this region. The estimate should depend on these feathers, and not on the water or the rock.
beats.caption: The second is grounding: where in the input is the evidence? For wingtip colour, it is this region. The estimate should depend on these feathers, and not on the water or the rock.
beats.head: Grounding: the evidence sits in one region of the {x:photo}

beats.text: The third is representation: how the concept becomes a number. The simplest is binary: c j is zero or one.
beats.caption: The third is representation: how the concept becomes a number. The simplest is binary: c j is zero or one.
beats.head: Representation: the simplest {c:concept} is binary

beats.text: A soft concept passes a logit, z, through the sigmoid, giving a value between zero and one. A logit of 1.4 gives 0.80.

beats.head: A soft {c:concept} turns a logit into a value between 0 and 1

beats.text: A soft score of 0.8 is not automatically a calibrated probability. Whether eighty percent of such cases really have grey wingtips has to be checked on data.

beats.text: How do concept values become an answer? In the simplest case, the task head is arithmetic small enough to do by hand.
beats.caption: How do concept values become an answer? In the simplest case, the task head is arithmetic small enough to do by hand.
beats.head: After the {c:concepts}, the {f:task head} is arithmetic you can do by hand

beats.text: Three classes: zebra, horse, and giraffe. Three concepts: stripes, horse-like shape, and long neck.
beats.caption: Three classes: zebra, horse, and giraffe. Three concepts: stripes, horse-like shape, and long neck.
beats.head: Three {y:classes} and three {c:concepts}

beats.text: Given this low-contrast photograph, the concept predictor reports stripes 0.1, horse-like shape 0.9, and long neck 0.1. Stacked in a column, they form the concept vector, c hat.
beats.caption: Given this low-contrast photograph, the concept predictor reports stripes 0.1, horse-like shape 0.9, and long neck 0.1. Stacked in a column, they form the concept vector, c hat.
beats.head: The {c:concept vector} $\cvec$ holds one value per concept

beats.text: The task head is a weight matrix, W, with one row per class. The zebra row holds 3 for stripes, 1 for horse-like shape, and 0 for long neck.
beats.caption: The task head is a weight matrix, W, with one row per class. The zebra row holds 3 for stripes, 1 for horse-like shape, and 0 for long neck.
beats.head: The {f:task head} keeps one row of weights for each {y:class}

beats.text: With all three rows: stripes count toward zebra, a long neck toward giraffe, and horse-like shape mostly toward horse.
beats.caption: With all three rows: stripes count toward zebra, a long neck toward giraffe, and horse-like shape mostly toward horse.
beats.head: The full {f:weight matrix} $\chead{W}$: rows are {y:classes}, columns are {c:concepts}

beats.text: To score zebra, multiply each weight by its concept value, and add. 3 times 0.1 is 0.3, 1 times 0.9 is 0.9, and 0 times 0.1 is 0. Zebra scores 1.2.
beats.caption: To score zebra, multiply each weight by its concept value, and add. 3 times 0.1 is 0.3, 1 times 0.9 is 0.9, and 0 times 0.1 is 0. Zebra scores 1.2.
beats.head: A {y:class score} is one row of {f:weights} times the {c:concept values}

beats.text: Horse: minus 0.1, plus 1.8, minus 0.1, giving 1.6. Giraffe: minus 0.1, plus 0, plus 0.3, giving 0.2. These are the class scores, or logits.
beats.caption: Horse: minus 0.1, plus 1.8, minus 0.1, giving 1.6. Giraffe: minus 0.1, plus 0, plus 0.3, giving 0.2. These are the class scores, or logits.
beats.head: Every row gives one {y:score}: $\cout{\mathbf{s}} = \chead{W}\cvec$

beats.text: The largest score is 1.6, so the model says horse. A softmax turns the scores into shares that sum to one: horse gets about 0.52.
beats.caption: The largest score is 1.6, so the model says horse. A softmax turns the scores into shares that sum to one: horse gets about 0.52.
beats.head: The largest {y:score} wins, and a softmax turns scores into shares

beats.caption: First, Concept Embedding Models. One number per concept is a narrow channel, and when the vocabulary is incomplete, accuracy suffers, as we saw in Part 8.
beats.head: One number per {c:concept} is a narrow channel

beats.text: Here is the intuition. Give each concept two prototypes, typical points that stand for stripes present and for stripes absent. The probability works like a dimmer switch that slides the concept between the two.
beats.caption: Here is the intuition. Give each concept two prototypes, typical points that stand for stripes present and for stripes absent. The probability works like a dimmer switch that slides the concept between the two.
beats.head: Intuition: two prototypes per {c:concept}, and a dimmer between them

beats.text: Both prototypes are computed from the image itself, so they can differ from one photo to the next. That lets detail beyond yes or no travel to the head.
beats.caption: Both prototypes are computed from the image itself, so they can differ from one photo to the next. That lets detail beyond yes or no travel to the head.
beats.head: The prototypes come from the {x:image}, so detail can travel

beats.text: Now the mechanics. An embedding is a short list of numbers that describes something; here each one has two numbers. From the image, the model computes two embeddings for every concept: one describing it as active, one as inactive.
beats.caption: Now the mechanics. An embedding is a short list of numbers that describes something; here each one has two numbers. From the image, the model computes two embeddings for every concept: one describing it as active, one as inactive.
beats.head: Each {c:concept} gets two embeddings: active and inactive

beats.text: It also predicts the probability, p, that the concept is present. Suppose that, as in Part 4, it misses the stripes on this photo: p is only 0.1.
beats.caption: It also predicts the probability, p, that the concept is present. Suppose that, as in Part 4, it misses the stripes on this photo: p is only 0.1.
beats.head: The model also predicts the probability {c:p} that the concept is present

beats.text: The concept's embedding mixes the two: p times the active embedding, plus one minus p times the inactive one.
beats.caption: The concept's embedding mixes the two: p times the active embedding, plus one minus p times the inactive one.
beats.head: The {c:concept embedding} mixes the two, weighted by {c:p}

beats.text: With p equal to 0.1, take the first entry: 0.1 times 0.82, plus 0.9 times 0.22, gives 0.28. The second entry works the same way, and the mixed vector sits close to inactive.

beats.head: With {c:p = 0.1}, the mixed vector sits close to inactive

beats.text: The head, a linear layer as in Part 4, reads all three concepts, six numbers in all. The stripes vector says inactive, so the head favours horse.
beats.caption: The head, a linear layer as in Part 4, reads all three concepts, six numbers in all. The stripes vector says inactive, so the head favours horse.

beats.text: During training, CEM randomly replaces some predicted probabilities with their true values, about one concept in four, so the head learns to respond to corrections.

beats.text: The gain is capacity: a vector can carry detail that one number cannot.
beats.caption: The gain is capacity: a vector can carry detail that one number cannot.
beats.head: Gain: a vector carries more than one number

beats.text: When does that matter? Recall Part 8. With only colour and size as concepts, the blue circle and the blue square got the same concept values, so no head could tell them apart.
beats.caption: When does that matter? Recall Part 8. With only colour and size as concepts, the blue circle and the blue square got the same concept values, so no head could tell them apart.

beats.text: With embeddings, the vector for blue is computed from each image, so it can differ between the circle and the square. Shape can then reach the head without ever being named.
beats.caption: With embeddings, the vector for blue is computed from each image, so it can differ between the circle and the square. Shape can then reach the head without ever being named.
beats.head: With embeddings, shape can reach the {f:head} without a name

beats.text: The cost is inspectability: the coordinates of that vector have no names, so part of what the head uses cannot be inspected. The detail that separated the circle from the square is exactly the part nobody can read.

beats.text: Compared with the plain CBM, two of the four things changed. Each concept is now a vector instead of one number, and the head reads those vectors. People still label every concept, and a trained predictor still detects them.

beats.text: Second, post-hoc concept bottleneck models. Instead of training a concept predictor from scratch, they reuse a pretrained encoder that already exists, so nobody labels concepts on the training images.
beats.caption: Second, post-hoc concept bottleneck models. Instead of training a concept predictor from scratch, they reuse a pretrained encoder that already exists, so nobody labels concepts on the training images.
beats.head: Reuse a {x:pretrained encoder}; no {c:concept labels} needed

beats.text: First, the intuition. A pretrained encoder already arranges photos in its feature space, and some directions in that space follow visual properties, such as how striped an animal is.
beats.caption: First, the intuition. A pretrained encoder already arranges photos in its feature space, and some directions in that space follow visual properties, such as how striped an animal is.
beats.head: Intuition: the {x:encoder} already arranges photos along directions

beats.text: A concept bank gives names to some of those directions. A concept score then asks one question: how far along the stripes direction is this photo?
beats.caption: A concept bank gives names to some of those directions. A concept score then asks one question: how far along the stripes direction is this photo?
beats.head: A {c:concept bank} names directions; a score asks how far along

beats.text: Now the details. Here the frozen encoder is CLIP's image encoder: each photograph becomes 512 numbers, which we call e of x.
beats.caption: Now the details. Here the frozen encoder is CLIP's image encoder: each photograph becomes 512 numbers, which we call e of x.
beats.head: A frozen {x:image encoder} turns each photo into 512 numbers

beats.text: Where does a direction come from? Yuksekgonul and colleagues use two routes. The first is a concept activation vector: separate the features of images with and without the concept by a linear boundary, and take the direction across it. It needs some labelled examples for each concept, but no labels on the training images.
beats.caption: Where does a direction come from? Yuksekgonul and colleagues use two routes. The first is a concept activation vector: separate the features of images with and without the concept by a linear boundary, and take the direction across it. It needs some labelled examples for each concept, but no labels on the training images.
beats.head: Route one to a {c:direction}: labelled examples (a CAV)

beats.text: The second route needs no example images at all. CLIP's text encoder places a phrase in the same space as the images, so the phrase itself gives the direction.
beats.caption: The second route needs no example images at all. CLIP's text encoder places a phrase in the same space as the images, so the phrase itself gives the direction.
beats.head: Route two: embed the concept's name with CLIP's {x:text encoder}

beats.text: We take the text route, with a concept bank of eight phrases, from black and white stripes to a wooden fence. Each phrase becomes a direction, v j.
beats.caption: We take the text route, with a concept bank of eight phrases, from black and white stripes to a wooden fence. Each phrase becomes a direction, v j.
beats.head: A {c:concept bank}: eight phrases, each a direction

beats.text: How far along a direction does a photo lie? Multiply the features and the direction entry by entry, then add up the products: this is the dot product. With just two entries, it is the first entry times the first, plus the second times the second.
beats.caption: How far along a direction does a photo lie? Multiply the features and the direction entry by entry, then add up the products: this is the dot product. With just two entries, it is the first entry times the first, plus the second times the second.
beats.head: A projection: multiply matching entries, then add

beats.text: A concept score is this projection, computed over all 512 entries, once for each of the eight directions. Both vectors have length one, so each score is also a cosine.
beats.caption: A concept score is this projection, computed over all 512 entries, once for each of the eight directions. Both vectors have length one, so each score is also a cosine.
beats.head: A {c:concept score} is the projection onto each direction

beats.text: A linear head is then trained with the class labels, on 24 photos. As in Part 4, each class score is a row of weights times the concept scores, plus a constant, b, and a softmax turns the scores into shares.

beats.text: The head is also sparse. An L1 penalty adds the size of every weight to the loss, so weights that do not help are pushed to exactly zero. Of 24 possible weights, 8 concepts times 3 classes, only 4 are non-zero: zebra reads stripes, giraffe reads a long neck, and horse reads a flowing mane.

beats.text: The hybrid version, PCBM-h, adds a residual: a second linear model that reads the raw features and recovers what the concepts miss. Its class scores are added to the head's scores before the softmax.
beats.caption: The hybrid version, PCBM-h, adds a residual: a second linear model that reads the raw features and recovers what the concepts miss. Its class scores are added to the head's scores before the softmax.
beats.head: PCBM-h adds a {k:residual} that reads the raw features

beats.text: Why does that help? Eight phrases cannot describe everything the encoder sees, and the residual picks up the rest. In the paper, PCBM-h comes close to the original model on every dataset reported, while the pure concept model falls further behind.
beats.caption: Why does that help? Eight phrases cannot describe everything the encoder sees, and the residual picks up the rest. In the paper, PCBM-h comes close to the original model on every dataset reported, while the pure concept model falls further behind.
beats.head: Why the {k:residual} helps accuracy

beats.text: The same side path weakens interventions. An edit changes a concept score, but the residual reads the raw features directly, so it keeps its vote for zebra whatever we write in the stripes slot.
beats.caption: The same side path weakens interventions. An edit changes a concept score, but the residual reads the raw features directly, so it keeps its vote for zebra whatever we write in the stripes slot.
beats.head: Why the {k:residual} weakens {e:interventions}

beats.text: On our photo, after the same edit, the hybrid still gives zebra 0.20 rather than 0.14, because part of its evidence never passed through a named concept.
beats.caption: On our photo, after the same edit, the hybrid still gives zebra 0.20 rather than 0.14, because part of its evidence never passed through a named concept.
beats.head: The {k:residual} is a side path that an {e:edit} cannot reach

beats.text: Compared with the plain CBM, three of the four things changed. The concepts come from a bank of phrases instead of people, a frozen encoder and a projection replace the trained predictor, and in the hybrid a residual also reaches the head. Each concept is still one number.

beats.text: The third variant is the label-free concept bottleneck model. A supervised bottleneck needs a person to label every concept on every photo, 112 of them for each bird in CUB. Label-free models need no human concept labels.

beats.text: Here is the intuition. CLIP is the teacher: it has learned from images paired with captions, so it can score how well any phrase matches any image. The student is a frozen ResNet with one linear layer on top, and it learns to copy the teacher's scores. A language model writes the exam questions: the phrases to score.
beats.caption: Here is the intuition. CLIP is the teacher: it has learned from images paired with captions, so it can score how well any phrase matches any image. The student is a frozen ResNet with one linear layer on top, and it learns to copy the teacher's scores. A language model writes the exam questions: the phrases to score.
beats.head: The intuition: a {x:student} learns to copy a {x:teacher}'s scores

beats.text: The method has five steps. The language model proposes phrases, CLIP filters and scores them, the student learns to copy the scores, and a sparse final layer, trained with the class labels, turns them into a class.
beats.caption: The method has five steps. The language model proposes phrases, CLIP filters and scores them, the student learns to copy the scores, and a sparse final layer, trained with the class labels, turns them into a class.

beats.text: Step one: ask a language model, for each class, for its most important features, the things commonly seen around it, and its superclasses, the broader groups it belongs to. Here is the real reply for zebra to the first question, as JSON.

beats.text: Step two: filter. Phrases that contain a class name go, such as zebras or horse-like body. Equine goes as a near-duplicate of equine animal. Leather saddle and ossicones on head go because even the photos that match them best score low with CLIP. 34 concepts remain.

beats.text: Step three: CLIP scores every image against every remaining concept. A higher score means the phrase fits the image better. These scores are the teacher's answers: targets for the student, not labels from a person.

beats.text: Step four builds the student. A different frozen network, here a ResNet-50 rather than CLIP, turns each image into 2048 features, written e of x. A linear layer, W c, maps them to 34 concept activations. This layer is often called the projection, and it is the only part that learns.

beats.text: What does copying mean? Take one concept, black and white stripes. Across many images, the student's activation should be high where CLIP's score is high, and low where it is low. Only this pattern across images matters, not the exact values.

beats.text: Before the comparison, every standardised value is cubed: multiplied by itself three times. Cubing stretches the extremes: a score two standard deviations above average becomes eight, while half a standard deviation shrinks to one eighth. So the images that CLIP scores highest count the most.

beats.text: To compare two lists of numbers, we use the cosine: multiply them entry by entry, add up, and divide by the two lengths. It is 1 when the lists rise and fall together, even if one is twice the other, near 0 when they are unrelated, and negative when they move in opposite directions.

beats.text: Why insist on sparsity? A dense layer would use all 102 weights, and nobody can check 102 numbers behind every decision. Six weights can be read in a few seconds, and each one is a claim a person can check, such as: black and white stripes count for zebra.

Stocky horse-like body matches another class better than zebras, so it separates nothing.

beats.text: For horse, a long flowing mane leads. For giraffe, an extremely long vertical neck.

beats.text: Step four: a linear layer from sentences to classes, started from a language prior, a starting guess taken from the sentences. Each class gives one third to each of its own three sentences, and nothing to the others.

beats.text: So each class score is the average of its own three sentence scores. For this zebra, zebra gets 28.1, horse 22.9 and giraffe 23.7. As shares, zebra gets 0.98, and 11 of the 12 test photos are right.

The prior already encodes it. A linear probe is a linear layer on CLIP's image features, with no concepts. The LaBo paper reports its clearest advantage over a linear probe with one labelled photo per class.

beats.text: Label-free models and LaBo share a weakness: nothing checks that a concept is actually visible in the image.
beats.caption: Label-free models and LaBo share a weakness: nothing checks that a concept is actually visible in the image.
beats.head: Nothing checks that a {c:concept} is really in the {x:image}

beats.text: The fix rests on a simple intuition. Naming a concept is not the same as pointing at it. So ask a detector to point at each concept in the image, and count only the concepts it can find.
beats.caption: The fix rests on a simple intuition. Naming a concept is not the same as pointing at it. So ask a detector to point at each concept in the image, and count only the concepts it can find.
beats.head: Naming a {c:concept} is not the same as pointing at it

beats.text: There are three ways a concept can fail. Some are not visual, such as a gull's call. Some describe the setting, not the bird. And some score highly on images that do not contain them, such as a black head on a gull whose head is white.
beats.caption: There are three ways a concept can fail. Some are not visual, such as a gull's call. Some describe the setting, not the bird. And some score highly on images that do not contain them, such as a black head on a gull whose head is white.

beats.text: Srivastava and colleagues point out that a head built on a set of random concepts can reach accuracy comparable to these models. So the concept scores were carrying information that their names do not describe, a form of the leakage we met in Part 9.

beats.text: Their method, VLG-CBM, grounds the concepts first. It uses an open-vocabulary object detector: a detector that can search for any phrase you give it, not only a fixed list of objects. It looks for each concept in each training image, and draws a box where it finds it.

beats.head: VLG-CBM asks a detector to find each {c:concept}

beats.text: A concept counts as present only where a box was found. For our gull, the bill, head and wingtips each get a one, and the call gets a zero. We call this vector c det: the concept labels from the detector.
beats.caption: A concept counts as present only where a box was found. For our gull, the bill, head and wingtips each get a one, and the call gets a zero. We call this vector c det: the concept labels from the detector.
beats.head: A box means 1, no box means 0

beats.text: These grounded labels train the concept layer: a linear layer that turns the backbone's features into one score per concept. The loss is a binary cross-entropy, as in the original CBM, but no person draws the labels.
beats.caption: These grounded labels train the concept layer: a linear layer that turns the backbone's features into one score per concept. The loss is a binary cross-entropy, as in the original CBM, but no person draws the labels.
beats.head: The {c:grounded labels} train the concept layer with a {l:loss}

beats.text: One term, as in Part 5. The wingtips have a box, so their label is one; if the layer predicts 0.8, the term is minus log 0.8, about 0.22. The call has no box, so its label is zero; a prediction of 0.2 costs the same, minus log of one minus 0.2.
beats.caption: One term, as in Part 5. The wingtips have a box, so their label is one; if the layer predicts 0.8, the term is minus log 0.8, about 0.22. The call has no box, so its label is zero; a prediction of 0.2 costs the same, minus log of one minus 0.2.
beats.head: One term of the {l:loss}, worked out

beats.text: They also report the number of effective concepts, NEC for short. Each row of the head holds one class's weights, one per concept. Count the non-zero weights in each row, here three, two and four, and average over the classes: the NEC is three.
beats.caption: They also report the number of effective concepts, NEC for short. Each row of the head holds one class's weights, one per concept. Count the non-zero weights in each row, here three, two and four, and average over the classes: the NEC is three.
beats.head: Count the non-zero {f:weights} in each class's row

beats.text: Why does this count matter? A head that puts weight on every concept can fit almost anything. The paper proves that even a random, untrained concept layer can approximate any linear classifier once there are enough concepts. So a dense head can be accurate and still explain nothing.

beats.text: So the fair comparison gives every model the same budget: the same number of concepts per class. Only then does higher accuracy say something about the concepts themselves.
beats.caption: So the fair comparison gives every model the same budget: the same number of concepts per class. Only then does higher accuracy say something about the concepts themselves.

beats.caption: In symbols, the count for class k is the zero norm of its row of weights: the number of entries that are not zero. The NEC averages that count over the K classes.
beats.head: The same count in symbols

beats.head: Five {c:concepts} per class can actually be read

beats.text: Compared with label-free models, two things change. The concept layer learns from the detector's boxes instead of copying CLIP's scores, and the head is judged at a fixed number of concepts per class.
beats.caption: Compared with label-free models, two things change. The concept layer learns from the detector's boxes instead of copying CLIP's scores, and the head is judged at a fixed number of concepts per class.
beats.head: What changed compared with {c:label-free} models

beats.text: In symbols: g is a backbone with a concept layer, W c, trained on the detector labels c det. f is sparse and linear, with the number of effective concepts held fixed. The data: images and class labels, plus a detector.
beats.caption: In symbols: g is a backbone with a concept layer, W c, trained on the detector labels c det. f is sparse and linear, with the number of effective concepts held fixed. The data: images and class labels, plus a detector.
beats.head: VLG-CBM in symbols

beats.text: The last step on the ladder removes training altogether. Menon and Vondrick call it classification by description.
beats.caption: The last step on the ladder removes training altogether. Menon and Vondrick call it classification by description.
beats.head: The last rung: no training data at all

beats.text: The intuition is a checklist. A language model writes a short checklist for every class. CLIP ticks each item softly, with a score for how well the photo matches it. The class with the best average tick wins.
beats.caption: The intuition is a checklist. A language model writes a short checklist for every class. CLIP ticks each item softly, with a score for how well the photo matches it. The class with the best average tick wins.
beats.head: Each {y:class} gets a checklist, and {x:CLIP} ticks it softly

beats.text: A language model writes a few descriptors for every class: short phrases about what the class looks like. For a herring gull: a white body with black wingtips, a yellow beak and legs, a red spot on its beak.
beats.caption: A language model writes a few descriptors for every class: short phrases about what the class looks like. For a herring gull: a white body with black wingtips, a yellow beak and legs, a red spot on its beak.
beats.head: A language model describes every {y:class}

beats.text: CLIP scores the image against each descriptor: that score is the soft tick. The class score is simply the average of its descriptors' scores, and the highest average wins.
beats.caption: CLIP scores the image against each descriptor: that score is the soft tick. The class score is simply the average of its descriptors' scores, and the highest average wins.
beats.head: {x:CLIP} scores the photo against each descriptor

beats.text: Where does a score come from? CLIP has two encoders. One, phi, turns the image into a vector; the other, psi, turns the descriptor into a vector in the same space. The score is the cosine similarity of the two: near one when they point the same way, smaller when they do not.
beats.caption: Where does a score come from? CLIP has two encoders. One, phi, turns the image into a vector; the other, psi, turns the descriptor into a vector in the same space. The score is the cosine similarity of the two: near one when they point the same way, smaller when they do not.
beats.head: One descriptor score: a {c:cosine} between two vectors

beats.text: Then y hat k, the score of class k, averages the descriptor scores over D k, the class's list of descriptors. Nothing is fitted to the target data.
beats.caption: Then y hat k, the score of class k, averages the descriptor scores over D k, the class's list of descriptors. Nothing is fitted to the target data.
beats.head: The {y:class score} averages its descriptor scores

beats.text: Every prediction comes with its reasons: the descriptor scores that were averaged. On our gull photograph, the five herring gull descriptors score between 0.32 and 0.34, and their average is about 0.33.
beats.caption: Every prediction comes with its reasons: the descriptor scores that were averaged. On our gull photograph, the five herring gull descriptors score between 0.32 and 0.34, and their average is about 0.33.
beats.head: Every score comes with its reasons

beats.text: But the slaty-backed gull's descriptors average slightly higher, so it edges ahead by a tiny margin. Our photo shows a herring gull, so this prediction is a near miss.
beats.caption: But the slaty-backed gull's descriptors average slightly higher, so it edges ahead by a tiny margin. Our photo shows a herring gull, so this prediction is a near miss.
beats.head: Slaty-backed gull edges ahead

beats.text: On all of CUB, the descriptors help only slightly over plain class names, where CLIP compares the photo with the species name alone: in our run, 53.1 percent against 52.9.
beats.caption: On all of CUB, the descriptors help only slightly over plain class names, where CLIP compares the photo with the species name alone: in our run, 53.1 percent against 52.9.
beats.head: On all of CUB, descriptors help only slightly

beats.text: So when is this attractive? When you have no labelled images at all. And a new class needs only a new description: write its checklist, and it can be scored at once, with no retraining.
beats.caption: So when is this attractive? When you have no labelled images at all. And a new class needs only a new description: write its checklist, and it can be scored at once, with no retraining.
beats.head: Attractive when there are no labels at all

beats.text: But the descriptors themselves can be wrong: the language model says a California gull has a black head, which it does not.
beats.caption: But the descriptors themselves can be wrong: the language model says a California gull has a black head, which it does not.
beats.head: A descriptor can be wrong

beats.text: That is one of several risks. A descriptor can also be non-visual: no single photo shows a bird's wingspan. It can describe the setting rather than the bird. And nobody checks the ticks: CLIP gives every item some score, true or not.
beats.caption: That is one of several risks. A descriptor can also be non-visual: no single photo shows a bird's wingspan. It can describe the setting rather than the bird. And nobody checks the ticks: CLIP gives every item some score, true or not.
beats.head: The risks: nobody checks the {c:checklist} or the ticks

beats.text: Compared with LaBo, the head is no longer learned. LaBo trained a linear layer on CLIP's sentence scores; here the class score is a fixed average, so nothing is trained and no labelled image is needed.
beats.caption: Compared with LaBo, the head is no longer learned. LaBo trained a linear layer on CLIP's sentence scores; here the class score is a fixed average, so nothing is trained and no labelled image is needed.
beats.head: What changed compared with LaBo: the {f:head} is no longer learned

scenes.title: How should we evaluate a CBM?

beats.text: How should we judge such a model? Accuracy alone hides most of what matters, so we ask four separate questions, each about a different part of the model.
beats.caption: How should we judge such a model? Accuracy alone hides most of what matters, so we ask four separate questions, each about a different part of the model.

beats.text: First, task accuracy: are the predictions correct? In everyday terms, is the final answer right? Measure it on held-out test images, images the model never saw during training.
beats.caption: First, task accuracy: are the predictions correct? In everyday terms, is the final answer right? Measure it on held-out test images, images the model never saw during training.

beats.text: The formula only counts. The bracket is 1 when the prediction matches the true label, and 0 when it does not. Add up the ones and divide by the number of images. Three predictions with two right give an accuracy of two thirds.
beats.caption: The formula only counts. The bracket is 1 when the prediction matches the true label, and 0 when it does not. Add up the ones and divide by the number of images. Three predictions with two right give an accuracy of two thirds.
beats.head: Task accuracy counts the right {y:answers}

beats.text: Second, concept accuracy: are the concept estimates correct? In everyday terms, did the model read the evidence correctly? Take one test image, a small red square. Round each concept score to 0 or 1, and compare it with the label. Large scores 0.78, which rounds to 1, but the square is small, so its label is 0. Four of the five match. Concept accuracy averages these matches over all images and all concepts.

beats.text: The second question has a second half, grounding: does each estimate rest on the intended evidence? A score for wingtip black should come from the wingtip, not from the water. So we also check where the detector looks.

beats.text: Third, faithfulness: does the output actually depend on the concepts, in the way the model claims? An explanation is faithful when it tells the truth about how the answer was made. beats.text: But the interface is only as good as its parts: the concepts it names, where they look, and the head that reads them. A concept may be missing, a detector may look at the water, and a head may hold a wrong rule.

beats.text: In short, concept bottleneck models put named values that people can read in the middle of a prediction. Those values can be inspected, evaluated, and sometimes corrected.

beats.text: The challenge is to make sure the interface faithfully represents the information on which the prediction depends. Put simply, whatever the answer uses should be visible in the concepts.

beats.head: The interface must carry what the {y:prediction} depends on

beats.text: Four things to remember. Post-hoc methods explain a model after the fact, while a concept bottleneck makes the answer pass through named concepts. Fixing a concept helps only if the head reads it the right way. A soft score can carry more than its name says, and that extra information leaks to the head. And newer variants find concepts with fewer labels, so check that each one looks at the right evidence.

scenes.title: Appendix: testing with concept activation vectors

beats.text: This appendix adds one more post-hoc method, one that asks about concepts directly. Testing with concept activation vectors, or TCAV, asks a question like this one: does the model use grey wings when it says herring gull? Here the model is CLIP, the black box from Part 1.
beats.caption: This appendix adds one more post-hoc method, one that asks about concepts directly. Testing with concept activation vectors, or TCAV, asks a question like this one: does the model use grey wings when it says herring gull? Here the model is CLIP, the black box from Part 1.
beats.head: TCAV asks about a named {c:concept}: does the model use {c:grey wings} when it says {y:herring gull}?

beats.text: The first step is to collect example photos: some birds with grey wings, and some without, here from a labelled bird dataset. None of them is a herring gull.
beats.caption: The first step is to collect example photos: some birds with grey wings, and some without, here from a labelled bird dataset. None of them is a herring gull.
beats.head: Step 1: collect photos {c:with grey wings} and photos {m:without}

beats.text: Pass every photo through the model and look at its internal activations. Fit a line that separates the two groups. The direction across that line is the concept activation vector: moving along it means more grey wing.
beats.caption: Pass every photo through the model and look at its internal activations. Fit a line that separates the two groups. The direction across that line is the concept activation vector: moving along it means more grey wing.
beats.head: Step 2: the {c:concept direction} separates them inside the model

beats.text: Now take a herring gull photo and ask: if its activation moved a little in the grey wing direction, would the herring gull score go up? The gradient of the score, times the direction, gives the answer as a sign.
beats.caption: Now take a herring gull photo and ask: if its activation moved a little in the grey wing direction, would the herring gull score go up? The gradient of the score, times the direction, gives the answer as a sign.
beats.head: Step 3: nudge each {y:herring gull} photo along that direction

beats.text: The TCAV score is the share of herring gull photos where the score goes up. For grey wings, it went up for almost all 60 photos, in each of 10 repeats with different example photos.
beats.caption: The TCAV score is the share of herring gull photos where the score goes up. For grey wings, it went up for almost all 60 photos, in each of 10 repeats with different example photos.
beats.head: The TCAV score: the share of photos whose {y:score} rises

beats.text: A direction that separates two random sets of photos gives scores that jump between zero and one. So a concept counts only when its score is steady and different from random ones. And even then, TCAV says what the model responds to. It gives no way to correct it.
